Bottom: line drawing of the face of a ring, inverted horizontally, divided into four quarters, with many human and animal figures in each.](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/dd/Ring_of_Nestor_Drawing_Evans_1925_with_Photo.png/250px-Ring_of_Nestor_Drawing_Evans_1925_with_Photo.png)

The **Ring of Nestor**[[a]](#cite_note-4) is a gold [signet ring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Signet_ring "Signet ring") first described by the archaeologist [Arthur Evans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arthur_Evans "Arthur Evans") in 1925. According to Evans, it was made on [Minoan Crete](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minoan_Crete "Minoan Crete") in the Late Bronze Age and discovered in a [Mycenaean tholos tomb](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tholos_tomb "Tholos tomb") near the ancient site of [Pylos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palace_of_Nestor "Palace of Nestor") in [Messenia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Messenia "Messenia"), in southwest Greece. The ring has a crowded and complex design, including human figures as well as real and mythical animals, and has been interpreted as indicating aspects of [Minoan religion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minoan_religion "Minoan religion"). Evans considered it to show scenes from the [underworld](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underworld "Underworld"), and to illustrate connections between Minoan belief and [ancient Egyptian religion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ancient_Egyptian_religion "Ancient Egyptian religion"). It is currently held by the [Ashmolean Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ashmolean_Museum "Ashmolean Museum") at the [University of Oxford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Oxford "University of Oxford"), to which Evans gifted it in 1939.

Since its discovery, the ring's authenticity has been debated, with several scholars considering it a modern fake, and others defending it as a genuinely ancient artefact. Arguments in both directions have been made on the grounds of iconographical consistency with other Minoan artworks, and based upon the potential role of [Émile Gilliéron *fils*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Émile_Gilliéron_fils "Émile Gilliéron fils"), an art restorer, suspected forger, and prolific collaborator of Evans's, in the ring's discovery. Other arguments for authenticity include the wear evident upon the ring and microscopic analysis of its engraving technique, while circumstantial evidence against it has been adduced from Evans's convoluted story of its origins and the fortuitous connections between its iconography and Evans's own ideas about the links between Minoan and Egyptian religion. The ring was removed from display at the Ashmolean in the 20th century, but returned to public view in 1995.

## Description

The authenticity of the Ring of Nestor is disputed.[[4]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHudler20194-5) Scholars who consider the ring to be ancient date it to the [Late Minoan I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Late_Minoan "Late Minoan") period (c. 1700 – c. 1450 BCE), during the [Neopalatial period](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neopalatial_Period "Neopalatial Period") of Minoan civilization.[[1]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGalanakis2013159-1) The ring is made of gold of 97% purity,[[5]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEVlachopoulos2020223-6) with the remaining 3% being made up of copper,[[1]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGalanakis2013159-1) and weighs 31.76 grams (1.12 oz).[[6]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGalanakis2013159Hughes-BrockBoardman2018448-7) It has a hollow [bezel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bezel "Bezel"),[[3]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHughes-BrockBoardman2018448-3) made of a gold sheet 0.25 mm (0.01 in) in thickness,[[7]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPini19988-8) with a groove for a finger set into the underside. The ring's hoop is decorated with a central band of [embossed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Embossing_(manufacturing) "Embossing (manufacturing)") hemispherical pieces,[[3]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHughes-BrockBoardman2018448-3) which are [soldered](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soldering "Soldering") onto the hoop,[[8]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPini19989-9) and with [granules](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granulation_(jewellery) "Granulation (jewellery)") of two different sizes. These pieces and granules have been deformed, with the most damage apparent on the central band of large hemispheres.[[3]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHughes-BrockBoardman2018448-3)

The hoop is slightly elliptical, with internal diameters of 1.4 and 1.56 cm (0.551 and 0.614 in), a width of 0.82 cm (0.32 in), and a thickness of 0.35 cm (0.14 in). The bezel is 3.29 cm (1.295 in) horizontally and 2.18 cm (0.858 in) vertically.[[3]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHughes-BrockBoardman2018448-3) Owing to the narrow diameter of the hoop, [Arthur Evans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arthur_Evans "Arthur Evans") (who first introduced the ring to scholarship) considered that it was probably intended to be hung on a string rather than worn on the finger.[[9]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEvans1930146-10)

The iconography on the ring's bezel is divided into four scenes, each occupying a quarter of the face. The scenes are separated by a thicker vertical band and a thinner horizontal band; the vertical band rises out of a base. At the intersection of the vertical band and the base is an animal form, whose identification has been debated. The bands are generally taken to represent the trunk and branches of a large tree.[[10]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTENilsson1927549–550-11) The bands were probably made with a [punch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punch_(tool) "Punch (tool)"), while the figures are likely to have been both punched and [engraved](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Engraving "Engraving").[[7]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPini19988-8)

Of the 99 known signet rings from the Aegean Bronze Age, the Ring of Nestor shows the greatest number of individual figures: it depicts fourteen human figures and at least five other animals.[[11]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEVlachopoulos2020228-12) In the scene in the upper-left quadrant, a lion can be seen lying on a large structure, called a "table" by Helen Hughes-Brock and [John Boardman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Boardman_(art_historian) "John Boardman (art historian)"), beneath which are two naked human women, each with one hand on the table. Four small branches, resembling [ivy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ivy "Ivy"), sprout from the vertical dividing-band to the image's right. Below this scene, several women in long, layered skirts can be seen: one walks towards the central band, while two approach a small table on which a [griffin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Griffin "Griffin") is seated. The women may have the heads of birds, or alternatively simply have their heads leant forwards. Behind the griffin, a female figure stands in a skirt slightly longer than those of the others, facing the ring's centre. Hughes-Brock and Boardman describe these two scenes as "otherworldly", in contrast to the scenes on the ring's right, which only contain human figures.[[12]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHughes-BrockBoardman2018448–449-13)

![Ancient wall painting: male figure, bare chested and wearing a kilt, carries a jug to the right](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/aa/%27Procession_Fresco%27_from_Knossos%2C_Neopalacial_period%2C_1600_-_1450_BC%2C_Heraklion_Archaeological_Museum_-_32931077207_crop.jpg/120px-%27Procession_Fresco%27_from_Knossos%2C_Neopalacial_period%2C_1600_-_1450_BC%2C_Heraklion_Archaeological_Museum_-_32931077207_crop.jpg)
![Ancient wall-painting: a woman, skin rendered in white, stoops to gather flowers: her hair is elaborately made up and she wears a many-layered skirt](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/11/Cueilleuse_de_safran%2C_fresque%2C_Akrotiri%2C_Gr%C3%A8ce.jpg/250px-Cueilleuse_de_safran%2C_fresque%2C_Akrotiri%2C_Gr%C3%A8ce.jpg)

On the right-hand side of the bezel, the upper image shows a pair of women, one sitting and one squatting, facing each other: one may be wearing a skirt, or both may be naked. Next to them are a man and a woman, standing; the man wears a belted [kilt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kilt "Kilt") and the woman a knee-length layered skirt. Above the human figures can be seen two winged insects and two ovoid shapes identified by Hughes-Brock and Boardman as [pupae](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pupa "Pupa"). Below this scene is one of four human figures walking towards the centre of the ring: the first and last figures are men, and the two in the middle are women in long, flounced skirts.[[12]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHughes-BrockBoardman2018448–449-13)

### Interpretation

Evans considered the ring to depict scenes from the Minoan [underworld](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underworld "Underworld"),[[13]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEvans192551-14) specifically "the admission of the departed into the realms of bliss".[[14]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEvans1930145-15) He interpreted the shape dividing the four quarters of the ring as "unquestionably a tree, old and gnarled", which he considered to be comparable with the [world tree](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_tree "World tree") called [Yggdrasil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yggdrasil "Yggdrasil") in [Norse mythology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norse_mythology "Norse mythology").[[15]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEvans192550–51-16) He considered the lion to be "the guardian of the [Lower World](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underworld "Underworld")",[[16]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEvans192514-17) and the creature at the base, which he took to be a dog, to be "the Minoan forerunner of [Cerberus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cerberus "Cerberus")"[[13]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEvans192551-14) – the three-headed dog who guards the underworld in classical Greek mythology.[[17]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEOgden2013109-18) The griffin on the bezel is a common motif in Minoan art, originally taken from the Near East.[[18]](#cite_note-19)

Evans wrote in a letter, shortly after seeing the ring, that it depicted "a map of the [Elysian Fields](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elysium "Elysium")" according to the Minoans.[[2]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMarinatosJackson20116-2) He interpreted the winged insects as butterflies, and as symbols of the [reincarnation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reincarnation "Reincarnation") of the human beings next to them. In the same scene, he saw the standing female figure as a goddess, and the male figure as a young man reunited with his lover, either after death or possibly upon entering the underworld while alive.[[19]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEvans1930151–152-20) He considered this goddess to be a [deity of the underworld](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chthonic_deities "Chthonic deities"), the lion (following parallels in Egyptian iconography) to be associated with her, and the two women in the same scene to be her handmaidens.[[20]](#cite_note-21) He described the scene with the griffin as that of souls being tested on entry to "the Halls of the Just in the Griffin's Court", and the griffin itself as a "Chief Inquisitor".[[21]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEvans1930154-22) Evans characterised the whole scene as "the abode of light rather than of darkness", equivalent to the paradise of Elysium in later Greek mythology.[[22]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEvans1930155–156-23) [Nanno Marinatos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nanno_Marinatos "Nanno Marinatos") and Briana Jackson suggest that Evans's interpretation of the scene via Egyptian mythology, as well as his reading of the central motif as a tree, was influenced by James Frazer's *[The Golden Bough](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Golden_Bough "The Golden Bough")*, as well as by the discovery of the [Tomb of Tutankhamun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tomb_of_Tutankhamun "Tomb of Tutankhamun") in 1923.[[23]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMarinatosJackson20119–10-24)

![Grey photograph of the cast of the ring's impression: as infobox image, except the creature at the base of the tree is highly indistinct](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/55/Ring_of_Nestor_Cast_Evans_1925.png/250px-Ring_of_Nestor_Cast_Evans_1925.png)

[Martin P. Nilsson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_P._Nilsson "Martin P. Nilsson") discussed the ring in a 1927 work on Minoan and Mycenaean religion, in which he called it "a most amazing find ... [which] differs most markedly from other Mycenaean rings".[[25]](#cite_note-26)[[b]](#cite_note-27) Nilsson disagreed with Evans's association between the tree motif and the world tree, pointing out that the motif was not known to be attested prior to the eighth century CE; he considered the tree more likely to prefigure the tree in the [Garden of the Hesperides](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Garden_of_the_Hesperides "Garden of the Hesperides") in Greek mythology, which grew golden apples.[[26]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTENilsson1927550-28) In support of this, he suggested that the creature labelled by Evans as a proto-Cerberus should be considered a forerunner of [Ladon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ladon_(mythology) "Ladon (mythology)"), the dragon who guarded that tree.[[27]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTENilsson1927551-29) He considered there to be no compelling reason to suggest that the scenes on the ring were related to the afterlife or the underworld.[[28]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTENilsson1927556-30) Galanakis identifies the figure as a dragon, and considers it to be inspired by similar [Babylonian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Babylon "Babylon") motifs otherwise rare in Minoan art;[[29]](#cite_note-31) Hughes-Brock and Boardman call it a "Minoan dragon".[[30]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHughes-BrockBoardman2018449-32) Andreas Vlachopoulos identifies it as a scorpion.[[11]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEVlachopoulos2020228-12)

[Jean-Claude Poursat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean-Claude_Poursat?action=edit&redlink=1 "Jean-Claude Poursat (page does not exist)") [[fr](https://fr.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean-Claude%20Poursat "fr:Jean-Claude Poursat")], in 1976, suggested that the vertical and horizontal bands represented rivers, a hypothesis initially entertained but dismissed by Evans. In support of this, Poursat argued that the creature at the base was a "fantastical crocodile" or "crocodile-dragon". He further suggested that the lower half of the bezel, assumed to be a single episode by Evans, may have been intended to show two successive scenes.[[31]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPoursat1976472-33) Olga Krzyszkowska described Evans's interpretation of the bezel as an underworld scene as "fanciful" in 2005.[[32]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKrzyszkowska2005334-34)

## History

![Line drawing of a gold ring, in three different orientations](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a9/Ring_of_Nestor_Side_Evans_1925.png/250px-Ring_of_Nestor_Side_Evans_1925.png)

In 1907, a series of [tholos tombs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tholos_tomb "Tholos tomb") at [Kakovatos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kakovatos "Kakovatos") in [Messenia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Messenia "Messenia"), in the southwest [Peloponnese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peloponnese_(region) "Peloponnese (region)") region of Greece, were excavated by the German archaeologist [Wilhelm Dörpfeld](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wilhelm_Dörpfeld "Wilhelm Dörpfeld").[[34]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEVlachopoulos2020224–225-36) According to Evans, the ring was taken by a local peasant from one of these tombs (along with blocks of masonry) prior to the excavation, probably from the grave-pit inside the tomb's chamber.[[35]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEvans192546-37)[[c]](#cite_note-39)

In 1924, or possibly earlier, the ring was shown to the acquisitions committee of the [National Archaeological Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Archaeological_Museum,_Athens "National Archaeological Museum, Athens") in Athens, of which the German archaeologist [Georg Karo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georg_Karo "Georg Karo") was a member.[[37]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMarinatos2015194-40) Following Karo's judgement, the committee rejected the ring as a forgery, created by a modern goldsmith in the early twentieth century.[[38]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEVlachopoulos2020226-41) Evans was subsequently informed of the ring's existence by somebody he described as "a trustworthy source" (and later "a friend"): Karo inferred that Evans was referring to [Émile Gilliéron *fils*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Émile_Gilliéron_fils "Émile Gilliéron fils"), an art restorer, suspected forger, and prolific collaborator of Evans's.[[39]](#cite_note-42) Nanno Marinatos endorsed this view in 2015,[[40]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMarinatos2015194–195-43) and Vlachopoulos called it "very possible" in 2020.[[41]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEVlachopoulos2020225-44)

Evans subsequently travelled to the Peloponnese to view the ring, where he was told that the finder had died, leaving the ring to his son; the son passed it into the possession of the owner of a nearby vineyard.[[35]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEvans192546-37) Evans purchased the ring from the vineyard owner between 1924 and 1925,[[42]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEvans192546Vlachopoulos2020225-45) and named it the "Ring of Nestor" after [the mythological king](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nestor_(mythology) "Nestor (mythology)") of [the region of Messenia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Messenia_(ancient_region) "Messenia (ancient region)") in the [Homeric](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homer "Homer") poems.[[2]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMarinatosJackson20116-2) He gifted the ring to the [Ashmolean Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ashmolean_Museum "Ashmolean Museum") at the [University of Oxford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Oxford "University of Oxford") in 1939.[[2]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMarinatosJackson20116-2) It was subsequently removed from display, though placed back there in 1995.[[43]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPini19981-46) As of 2018, it remains in the Ashmolean.[[3]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHughes-BrockBoardman2018448-3)

## Debate over authenticity

The authenticity of the Ring of Nestor has been debated since its introduction to scholarship. In 2019, Angelika Hudler categorised the ring among *gemmae dubitandae* ('jewels deserving scepticism').[[d]](#cite_note-48)[[4]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHudler20194-5) In 2013, Yannis Galanakis called the ring "one of the most controversial Aegean objects in the Ashmolean's collection".[[1]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGalanakis2013159-1)

### Arguments against authenticity

Before the 1970s, most scholars considered the ring a forgery.[[45]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEliopoulos2013210-49) Nilsson, who treated the ring as genuine in 1927, revised the 1950 edition of his work to call it a "suspect object".[[46]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHudler20196-50) According to [Nanno Marinatos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nanno_Marinatos "Nanno Marinatos"), her father [Spyridon Marinatos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spyridon_Marinatos "Spyridon Marinatos") considered the Ring of Nestor a fake. She cites as evidence a reference in a 1928 letter by Marinatos to "reprimands" Evans was receiving about forgeries.[[47]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMarinatos2015190–191-51) Hagen Biesantz argued in 1954 that the ring's iconography was inconsistent with the known corpus of [Minoan art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minoan_art "Minoan art"), and accordingly that the ring was a forgery.[[48]](#cite_note-52)

![A gold ring, like the Ring of Nestor, with an oval bezel inscribed with figures. A youth climbs a hill in the centre to pick something from a tree, while two seated female figures watch.](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c1/Epiphany_cycle_%E2%80%94_THE_RING_OF_MINOS.jpg/250px-Epiphany_cycle_%E2%80%94_THE_RING_OF_MINOS.jpg)

Evans published the ring alongside the "Thisbe Treasure" from [Boeotia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boeotia "Boeotia"), considered a modern forgery, and the connection has cast doubt upon the Ring of Nestor in turn.[[32]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKrzyszkowska2005334-34) John Younger, in 1975, suggested that the ring had been forged by Gilliéron *fils* and [his father](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Émile_Gilliéron "Émile Gilliéron"), who had also been accused of forging the [Ring of Minos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ring_of_Minos?action=edit&redlink=1 "Ring of Minos (page does not exist)") apparently found at Knossos and also published by Evans.[[49]](#cite_note-53) In 1986,[[43]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPini19981-46) the Swedish archaeologist [Robin Hägg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robin_Hägg?action=edit&redlink=1 "Robin Hägg (page does not exist)") [[sv](https://sv.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robin%20Hägg "sv:Robin Hägg")] separately reported hearing from a collaborator of [Axel W. Persson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Axel_W._Persson "Axel W. Persson"), who had worked on the Aegean Bronze Age in the 1930s, that Persson had told her that Gilliéron *fils* had forged the Ring of Nestor: Hägg subsequently heard the same story from the Egyptologist [Torgny Säve-Söderbergh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Torgny_Säve-Söderbergh "Torgny Säve-Söderbergh") and from [Doro Levi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doro_Levi "Doro Levi"), director of the [Italian School of Archaeology at Athens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Italian_School_of_Archaeology_at_Athens "Italian School of Archaeology at Athens") from 1947 until 1976.[[50]](#cite_note-54) [Agnes Sakellariou](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agnes_Sakellariou?action=edit&redlink=1 "Agnes Sakellariou (page does not exist)") upheld the Gilliéron hypothesis in 1994, arguing that the insects labelled as butterflies by Evans had no direct parallels in Minoan art, but could have been based by a forger on Mycenaean examples found in tombs on the Greek mainland.[[51]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPini19983–5-55) Krzyszkowska similarly accused the Gilliérons of forging the ring in 2005.[[52]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKrzyszkowska2005p._336,_n._113-56)

Nanno Marinatos and Briana Jackson wrote in 2011 that the "complicated chain of transmission" reported to Evans raised suspicion, and made it impossible to verify the truth of the ring's discovery.[[53]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMarinatosJackson20117-57) They also argued that butterflies had no connection to the soul or reincarnation in Minoan culture, but that they were included on the ring because they held this metaphorical function in Victorian thought, and had been incorrectly linked to the concept in Mycenaean culture by [Heinrich Schliemann](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heinrich_Schliemann "Heinrich Schliemann") and more widely in Frazer's work.[[54]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMarinatosJackson201111–12-58) Marinatos and Jackson suggested that the connections between the ring's design and Egyptian iconography were based directly on *The Golden Bough*, which emphasised the religious role of oak trees and [mistletoe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mistletoe "Mistletoe"), and calculated to appeal to Evans, who had long sought to establish a relationship between Minoan religion and that of ancient Egypt.[[55]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMarinatosJackson201110-59)

### Arguments in favour of authenticity

[V. Gordon Childe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/V._Gordon_Childe "V. Gordon Childe") wrote in 1925 that "fortunately no such suspicions [of forgery] attach to the unique gold ring", and that it was "undoubtedly a remnant of the regal wealth once buried in the great tombs of Kakovatos".[[56]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChilde1925636-60)[[e]](#cite_note-62) Yiannis Sakellarakis, in 1973, considered the iconography of the ring to match other known Minoan examples, and so that the ring was likely to be genuine.[[58]](#cite_note-63) Jean-Claude Poursat accepted these arguments in his own publication of 1976.[[31]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPoursat1976472-33)

![Colourful drawing in the style of a Minoan fresco, replicating the bezel of the Ring of Nestor. The creature at the bottom of the tree is rendered as an oddly-posed dog.](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/91/Ring_of_Nestor_Drawing_Evans_1928.png/250px-Ring_of_Nestor_Drawing_Evans_1928.png)

Vlachopoulos suggests that Gilliéron could not have been involved in faking the ring, because his drawing of the bezel for Evans's publications showed a hound for the creature Vlachopoulos identified as a scorpion, demonstrating "his ignorance and his innocence".[[11]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEVlachopoulos2020228-12) [Ingo Pini](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ingo_Pini?action=edit&redlink=1 "Ingo Pini (page does not exist)") [[de](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ingo%20Pini "de:Ingo Pini")] similarly argued that the different treatment of the creature on the ring and Gilliéron's later painting of the same scene, in which Pini described the rendering as "a rather odd-looking quadruped", indicates that Gilliéron could not have made both.[[59]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPini19986-64)

Similarly, Theodore Eliopoulos suggested that the "table" on which the lion reclines as a horizontal platform supported by three incurved altars: such a platform was unknown in Minoan iconography at the time of the ring's discovery,[[60]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEliopoulos2013212–214-65) but later found in the 1970s and 1980s on frescoes from [Akrotiri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Akrotiri_(prehistoric_city) "Akrotiri (prehistoric city)"). Eliopoulos considers this evidence for a genuine Bronze Age origin.[[61]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEliopoulos2013221-66) Similarly, he argues that the appearance of lions as supporters of goddesses, known from Akrotiri frescoes as well as rings and sealings discovered after 1925, suggest the authenticity of the ring, as the lion's presence was considered anomalous when the ring was first published.[[62]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEliopoulos2013219-67) Pini argued against Sakellariou's interpretation of the butterflies as without precedent, suggesting that they echoed sealings found at the Cretan site of [Hagia Triada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hagia_Triada "Hagia Triada"), excavated in 1902–1903 but not published until 1925.[[63]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPini19985-68) He also drew a parallel between the creature at the base of the tree, which he called a "Minoan dragon", and a form on a seal found at [Mycenae](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mycenae "Mycenae") in the 1990s, while arguing that the motif would not have been known to a forger in the early twentieth century.[[59]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPini19986-64)

In 1998, [Jack Ogden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jack_Ogden_(jewellery_historian) "Jack Ogden (jewellery historian)") studied the manufacturing technique of the ring, and concluded that it matched that of genuine examples, whereby the bezel was carved first, the hoop added, and the back plate of the bezel then soldered into place. In addition, he considered that microscopic analysis of the engraving showed that it had been done according to Mycenaean techniques, which would have been unknown to an early twentieth-century forger.[[64]](#cite_note-69) Ultrasound scans of the ring presented by Walter Müller in 2002 confirmed that it was hollow, dispelling a longstanding belief that it was solid in construction, which would be unusual for a genuinely Bronze Age ring.[[65]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMüller2003480Krzyszkowska2005p._334,_n._111-70) Pini suggested that the wear on the decorations of the hoop indicates intensive use, and parallels other rings known to be genuine.[[66]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPini199810-71) Childe similarly suggested that the wear on these parts may suggest that the ring was actually worn, in contrast to Evans's belief.[[56]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChilde1925636-60)

Kate Cooper, in 2021, wrote that the ring was generally considered fake, but that the 2015 discovery of a ring (designated Ring 2) in the [Tomb of the Griffin Warrior](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tomb_of_the_Griffin_Warrior "Tomb of the Griffin Warrior"), a [shaft grave](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shaft_grave "Shaft grave") at Pylos dating to the [Late Helladic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Late_Helladic "Late Helladic") IIA period (c. 1400 – c. 1300 BCE) with similar iconography, particularly the ivy, pointed towards its authenticity.[[67]](#cite_note-72)

# *The Ring of Nestor: a Glimpse into the Minoan After-World and a Sepulchral Treasure of Gold Signet-Rings and Bead-Seals from Thisbe, Boeotia*

[*Nature*](/)
**volume 116**, pages 635–636 (1925) [Cite this article](#citeas)

215 Accesses

3 Altmetric

[Metrics details](/articles/116635a0/metrics)

## Abstract

TO-DAY even the most old-fashioned admirer of Hellenism has to admit that classical Greek civilisation was not only preceded by but also actually rooted in the Minoan culture of Crete and its continental daughter, the Mycenaean. The excavator of Minos' palace at Knossos, who so dramatically found the key to the riddle of pre-classical Greece, has himself taken the lead in tracing the influence of the Minoan civilisation on the classical; again and again he has illuminated the dark background of Hellenic life by a reference to the remains of the prehistoric age or interpreted the monuments of that still dumb epoch from the records of historic Greece.

The Ring of Nestor: a Glimpse into the Minoan After-World and a Sepulchral Treasure of Gold Signet-Rings and Bead-Seals from Thisbe, Boeotia.

By Sir Arthur Evans. Pp. ii + 75 + 5 plates. (London: Macmillan and Co., Ltd., 1925.) 12*s*. 6*d*. net.

## Abstract

![Image 10: sparkles](https://a.academia-assets.com/images/icons/sparkle.svg)
AI

This paper presents an analysis of the iconography surrounding the 'Ring of Nestor' in the context of Aegean forgeries and authenticity debates. By revisiting key iconographic features and comparisons, the paper aims to contribute to the ongoing discourse regarding the ring's significance in Minoan and Mycenaean art. Observations draw upon historical scholarship and recent discoveries to question and affirm previous conclusions related to the ring's motifs and their implications.

![Image 11: sparkles](https://a.academia-assets.com/images/icons/sparkle.svg)
AI

1.   The text explores the authenticity of the 'Ring of Nestor' through iconographic analysis.
2.   Contradictions in technical analysis highlight the importance of iconography in Aegean studies.
3.   The connection between incurved altars and the ring's depiction supports its authenticity.
4.   The ring's iconography may reflect cultural practices from the 1920s.
5.   Generations of scholars have debated the genuineness of both Nestor's and Minos' rings.

[Towards a Consideration of Unprovenanced Ancient and Medieval Finger Rings](https://www.academia.edu/37745254/Towards_a_Consideration_of_Unprovenanced_Ancient_and_Medieval_Finger_Rings)

[TN Pollio](https://independent.academia.edu/TNPollio)

This article will hopefully incentivize researchers to consider examining the untoward thousands of unprovenanced base metal and silver alloy finger rings being uncovered at sites from the U.K to Eurasia. Documented artifacts from controlled and stratified environments are of course essential towards understanding ring typology and routes of transmission across temporal and spatial environments. However, these standard methodologies should not preclude consideration of random and under-documented finds from non-professional sources. The rationale is simply that, within the last several decades, a significant proportion of new finds have in fact been made through amateur channels; and the rings they've uncovered may potentially contribute to our understanding of these underreported artifacts. Within the last few decades, the proliferation of metal detecting and use of the internet have ensured the issue is no longer of availability, but identity. The era of scarcity is obviously over, in view of the burgeoning array of base metal rings encountered on the international market. Any a priori disqualification of such a vast resource of emerging data is to ignore an untapped resource towards our understanding of ancient societies and the material culture associated therewith The need for reliable and broadly accessible reference material becomes increasingly apparent as more and more finger rings are uncovered and presented through on-line and other sources. Types which were once familiar only to academics have suddenly flooded the public conscience; but with little increase in resources towards the understanding of these artifacts. Small finds such as bronze finger rings are routinely uncovered at archaeological sites in Europe, North Africa, the Middle East and Eurasia. They are typically noted in excavation reports, then cataloged and archived in places such as universities and museums. Unfortunately, both the reports and rings themselves are rarely accessible in mediums available to the general public. In most cases, only other professionals – such as academics and historians – are even aware of their existence. In terms of accessibility, most of this research has been compiled in unfamiliar languages and arcane formats which, to the general public, might as well be written in cuneiform and buried on the dark side of the moon. Many in English speaking countries have some proficiency in languages such as French, German and Spanish. But how many would understand technical reports written in Russian, Polish, Slovak, Bulgarian, Serbian, Romanian, Hungarian, Turkish or Greek – the languages in which much of this research has been published? Unfamiliar languages and limited/restricted formats are significant impediments toward the dissemination of this otherwise invaluable material.

[One Ring to Know Them All: An Experimental Approach to Reconstructing the 'Ring of Hermes'](https://www.academia.edu/122737531/One_Ring_to_Know_Them_All_An_Experimental_Approach_to_Reconstructing_the_Ring_of_Hermes)

[Marios Koutsoukos](https://liverpool.academia.edu/MariosKoutsoukos)

Work In Progress, 2023

In Late Antiquity, no Roman would think twice about questioning the efficacy of ceremonial magic. They might doubt its legitimacy or, perhaps, the methods of the magician, but no one would ever dismiss magic itself as an operative force in the cosmos as well as a direct means of interacting with divine powers. Its potential efficacy was an accepted reality of life for layman and philosopher alike. It is in this cultural milieu that magical formularies such as those preserved in the Greek Magical Papyri circulated amongst ritual experts and Platonic philosophers with an affinity towards theurgy. What was the magical praxis like from the perspective of the operator? How did it enable a direct interaction with divine powers from a lived ancient religions point of view? When addressing these questions, modern scholarship very often confines itself in the traditional approach of textual examination, relying on individual accounts, such as that of the first-century Greek physician Thessalos of Tralles. or second-hand narratives, like those in Porphyry’s Life of Plotinus. The present paper proposes a hybrid method of studying Late Antique magical formularies which combines the methodology of textual approach with that of experimental archaeology. Termed experimental ritualism, this approach is presented through an experiment in reconstructing the magic ‘Ring of Hermes’ (PGM 213-303). This paper uses self-reflection to trace the process from the construction of the physical object itself to its ritual consecration and the attempts at putting the ring to its intended use. In effect, it is not merely the record of an experimental reconstruction but also an attempt at empirically adopting as emic a perspective as possible towards Late Antique magic praxis. Keywords: Graeco-Egyptian Magic; Greek Magical Papyri; Late Antiquity; Experimental Archaeology; Theurgy; Magic Ring.

The task of attributing seals to different hands or workshops is still a desideratum in Aegean studies, for the identification of Aegean seal-engravers and goldsmiths and their stylistic output could dramatically change our knowledge of the use, circulation and social impact of certain seals or seal groups and refine our methods of dating this (often only roughly datable) medium. A set of new data and methods now available, such as precise measurements of sizes and weights, x-ray analysis and material analysis finally enable us to shed new light on several questions concerning individual styles and thus to identify " masters " without the usual reliance on iconography. In this article, a set of thirteen signets will be presented in a detailed study highlighting their find contexts, their technical criteria and their iconographical similarities, leading to the conclusion that the rings were very probably made by six different " masters " working in the phases LH II – LH IIIA on Crete and the Greek mainland.

Jerusalem Journal of Archaeology

This paper presents a rare bronze finger ring that was found more than half a century ago and bears a symbol known mainly from the coins of Mattathias Antigonus. A teenager recovered it from one of the burial caves in the cliff of Naḥal David at ‘En Gedi. Although the cave was later excavated by Nahman Avigad, the ring was forgotten and was not incorporated in the excavation report. This paper discusses the ring, the symbol it bears, and its relation to the coins of Antigonus. I suggest a date and identification for the burials in the cave that associates them with the conflict between Herod and Antigonus.

The many years of research that led to the present paper on the so-called Ring of Nestor (CMS VI, nο. 277), with the documentation of its authenticity, have offered me the opportunity to discuss the cases of erroneous identifications of some Creto-Mycenaean gold rings as fakes . This tendency, underpinned by the obscure – even legendary – circumstances in which these rings were found, not only the Ring of Nestor but also the Ring of Minos, has been reassessed completely in favour of their authenticity. This revision has been significantly reinforced by recent finds of iconographic subjects of comparable resonance (wall-paintings, gold rings, figurines, ivories, and so on), as well as by more thorough study of the techniques and craftsmanship of these unique signet rings of the first centuries of the Late Bronze Age (16th-15th century BC). The key pictorial unit of the Ring of Nestor examined in this paper is Evans’s “watch-dog” or “dragon”, namely the guardian of the old “tree of the world”, whose branches host the most populous scene in Aegean glyptic art. This motif is here identified as a scorpion, a major apotropaic symbol in Bronze Αge Aegean iconography, which kills the “Μinoan Dragon” of the ring and offers a sound interpretation of the ring’s iconography.

[Sam Crooks](https://independentresearcher.academia.edu/SamCrooks), [Caroline J . Tully](https://unimelb.academia.edu/CarolineTully)

A group of Late Minoan signet rings fashioned in precious metals and engraved with complex and evocative iconographic schemes appears to depict ‘nature’ or ‘rural’ cults enacted at extra-urban sanctuaries, and may have functioned as inalienable possessions implicated in the expression and maintenance of elite identities during the Aegean Bronze Age. The images on the ring bezels depict human figures in association with epiphanic figures situated in settings characterised by the presence of trees and stones, columnar shrines, stepped altars, openwork platforms, tripartite shrines and sanctuary walls, perhaps involving occasional rites and the erection and dismantling of temporary cult structures which can themselves be viewed as architectonic replications of rural cult sites and natural forms. Just as the fabric of these rings and the artistry and technical skill of their production were of restricted accessibility and controlled distribution, we may infer that so, too, the rites, places and activities recorded on these rings were socially restricted. Possession of these distinctive and desirable objects of economic, cultural and symbolic value may have signified access to, involvement in and mastery over such rituals, the special status of the owner delineated and broadcast through the circulating media of clay sealings, advertising their special relationship with forces and places within nature. Over time the personal and cultural memory, knowledge and associations accumulated within these rings may form histories or biographies of the rings themselves, implicating the identities of their past and present owners, and of the wider community. In this way, they can be understood as inalienable possessions, objects invested with authority and authenticity that in turn authenticate the status of their owners. These enduring symbols draw the past into the present, instantiating cultural and cosmological ideals which classify and objectify social relations through referencing the past. Thus these rings function as mnemonic devices, palimpsests of memory, association and affect which store and transmit information about spatially and temporally disbursed places, people and events, memorialising and broadcasting elite association with the (super)natural world and forming part of the material affordances of the world of things which recursively produce, reiterate and transform identities through ecologies of practice: the past mediated in the present through memory materialised in objects.

# Ring of Nestor

![Top: Photograph of a gold ring, engraved with a complex design. Bottom: line drawing of the face of a ring, inverted horizontally, divided into four quarters, with many human and animal figures in each.](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/dd/Ring_of_Nestor_Drawing_Evans_1925_with_Photo.png/250px-Ring_of_Nestor_Drawing_Evans_1925_with_Photo.png)

The **Ring of Nestor**[[a]](#cite_note-4) is a gold [signet ring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Signet_ring "Signet ring") first described by the archaeologist [Arthur Evans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arthur_Evans "Arthur Evans") in 1925. According to Evans, it was made on [Minoan Crete](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minoan_Crete "Minoan Crete") in the Late Bronze Age and discovered in a [Mycenaean tholos tomb](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tholos_tomb "Tholos tomb") near the ancient site of [Pylos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palace_of_Nestor "Palace of Nestor") in [Messenia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Messenia "Messenia"), in southwest Greece. The ring has a crowded and complex design, including human figures as well as real and mythical animals, and has been interpreted as indicating aspects of [Minoan religion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minoan_religion "Minoan religion"). Evans considered it to show scenes from the [underworld](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underworld "Underworld"), and to illustrate connections between Minoan belief and [ancient Egyptian religion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ancient_Egyptian_religion "Ancient Egyptian religion"). It is currently held by the [Ashmolean Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ashmolean_Museum "Ashmolean Museum") at the [University of Oxford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Oxford "University of Oxford"), to which Evans gifted it in 1939.

Since its discovery, the ring's authenticity has been debated, with several scholars considering it a modern fake, and others defending it as a genuinely ancient artefact. Arguments in both directions have been made on the grounds of iconographical consistency with other Minoan artworks, and based upon the potential role of [Émile Gilliéron *fils*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Émile_Gilliéron_fils "Émile Gilliéron fils"), an art restorer, suspected forger, and prolific collaborator of Evans's, in the ring's discovery. Other arguments for authenticity include the wear evident upon the ring and microscopic analysis of its engraving technique, while circumstantial evidence against it has been adduced from Evans's convoluted story of its origins and the fortuitous connections between its iconography and Evans's own ideas about the links between Minoan and Egyptian religion. The ring was removed from display at the Ashmolean in the 20th century, but returned to public view in 1995.

## Description

The authenticity of the Ring of Nestor is disputed.[[4]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHudler20194-5) Scholars who consider the ring to be ancient date it to the [Late Minoan I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Late_Minoan "Late Minoan") period (c. 1700 – c. 1450 BCE), during the [Neopalatial period](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neopalatial_Period "Neopalatial Period") of Minoan civilization.[[1]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGalanakis2013159-1) The ring is made of gold of 97% purity,[[5]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEVlachopoulos2020223-6) with the remaining 3% being made up of copper,[[1]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGalanakis2013159-1) and weighs 31.76 grams (1.12 oz).[[6]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGalanakis2013159Hughes-BrockBoardman2018448-7) It has a hollow [bezel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bezel "Bezel"),[[3]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHughes-BrockBoardman2018448-3) made of a gold sheet 0.25 mm (0.01 in) in thickness,[[7]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPini19988-8) with a groove for a finger set into the underside. The ring's hoop is decorated with a central band of [embossed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Embossing_(manufacturing) "Embossing (manufacturing)") hemispherical pieces,[[3]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHughes-BrockBoardman2018448-3) which are [soldered](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soldering "Soldering") onto the hoop,[[8]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPini19989-9) and with [granules](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granulation_(jewellery) "Granulation (jewellery)") of two different sizes. These pieces and granules have been deformed, with the most damage apparent on the central band of large hemispheres.[[3]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHughes-BrockBoardman2018448-3)

The hoop is slightly elliptical, with internal diameters of 1.4 and 1.56 cm (0.551 and 0.614 in), a width of 0.82 cm (0.32 in), and a thickness of 0.35 cm (0.14 in). The bezel is 3.29 cm (1.295 in) horizontally and 2.18 cm (0.858 in) vertically.[[3]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHughes-BrockBoardman2018448-3) Owing to the narrow diameter of the hoop, [Arthur Evans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arthur_Evans "Arthur Evans") (who first introduced the ring to scholarship) considered that it was probably intended to be hung on a string rather than worn on the finger.[[9]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEvans1930146-10)

The iconography on the ring's bezel is divided into four scenes, each occupying a quarter of the face. The scenes are separated by a thicker vertical band and a thinner horizontal band; the vertical band rises out of a base. At the intersection of the vertical band and the base is an animal form, whose identification has been debated. The bands are generally taken to represent the trunk and branches of a large tree.[[10]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTENilsson1927549–550-11) The bands were probably made with a [punch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punch_(tool) "Punch (tool)"), while the figures are likely to have been both punched and [engraved](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Engraving "Engraving").[[7]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPini19988-8)

Of the 99 known signet rings from the Aegean Bronze Age, the Ring of Nestor shows the greatest number of individual figures: it depicts fourteen human figures and at least five other animals.[[11]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEVlachopoulos2020228-12) In the scene in the upper-left quadrant, a lion can be seen lying on a large structure, called a "table" by Helen Hughes-Brock and [John Boardman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Boardman_(art_historian) "John Boardman (art historian)"), beneath which are two naked human women, each with one hand on the table. Four small branches, resembling [ivy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ivy "Ivy"), sprout from the vertical dividing-band to the image's right. Below this scene, several women in long, layered skirts can be seen: one walks towards the central band, while two approach a small table on which a [griffin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Griffin "Griffin") is seated. The women may have the heads of birds, or alternatively simply have their heads leant forwards. Behind the griffin, a female figure stands in a skirt slightly longer than those of the others, facing the ring's centre. Hughes-Brock and Boardman describe these two scenes as "otherworldly", in contrast to the scenes on the ring's right, which only contain human figures.[[12]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHughes-BrockBoardman2018448–449-13)

![Ancient wall painting: male figure, bare chested and wearing a kilt, carries a jug to the right](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/aa/%27Procession_Fresco%27_from_Knossos%2C_Neopalacial_period%2C_1600_-_1450_BC%2C_Heraklion_Archaeological_Museum_-_32931077207_crop.jpg/120px-%27Procession_Fresco%27_from_Knossos%2C_Neopalacial_period%2C_1600_-_1450_BC%2C_Heraklion_Archaeological_Museum_-_32931077207_crop.jpg)
![Ancient wall-painting: a woman, skin rendered in white, stoops to gather flowers: her hair is elaborately made up and she wears a many-layered skirt](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/11/Cueilleuse_de_safran%2C_fresque%2C_Akrotiri%2C_Gr%C3%A8ce.jpg/250px-Cueilleuse_de_safran%2C_fresque%2C_Akrotiri%2C_Gr%C3%A8ce.jpg)

On the right-hand side of the bezel, the upper image shows a pair of women, one sitting and one squatting, facing each other: one may be wearing a skirt, or both may be naked. Next to them are a man and a woman, standing; the man wears a belted [kilt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kilt "Kilt") and the woman a knee-length layered skirt. Above the human figures can be seen two winged insects and two ovoid shapes identified by Hughes-Brock and Boardman as [pupae](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pupa "Pupa"). Below this scene is one of four human figures walking towards the centre of the ring: the first and last figures are men, and the two in the middle are women in long, flounced skirts.[[12]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHughes-BrockBoardman2018448–449-13)

### Interpretation

Evans considered the ring to depict scenes from the Minoan [underworld](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underworld "Underworld"),[[13]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEvans192551-14) specifically "the admission of the departed into the realms of bliss".[[14]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEvans1930145-15) He interpreted the shape dividing the four quarters of the ring as "unquestionably a tree, old and gnarled", which he considered to be comparable with the [world tree](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_tree "World tree") called [Yggdrasil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yggdrasil "Yggdrasil") in [Norse mythology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norse_mythology "Norse mythology").[[15]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEvans192550–51-16) He considered the lion to be "the guardian of the [Lower World](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underworld "Underworld")",[[16]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEvans192514-17) and the creature at the base, which he took to be a dog, to be "the Minoan forerunner of [Cerberus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cerberus "Cerberus")"[[13]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEvans192551-14) – the three-headed dog who guards the underworld in classical Greek mythology.[[17]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEOgden2013109-18) The griffin on the bezel is a common motif in Minoan art, originally taken from the Near East.[[18]](#cite_note-19)

Evans wrote in a letter, shortly after seeing the ring, that it depicted "a map of the [Elysian Fields](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elysium "Elysium")" according to the Minoans.[[2]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMarinatosJackson20116-2) He interpreted the winged insects as butterflies, and as symbols of the [reincarnation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reincarnation "Reincarnation") of the human beings next to them. In the same scene, he saw the standing female figure as a goddess, and the male figure as a young man reunited with his lover, either after death or possibly upon entering the underworld while alive.[[19]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEvans1930151–152-20) He considered this goddess to be a [deity of the underworld](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chthonic_deities "Chthonic deities"), the lion (following parallels in Egyptian iconography) to be associated with her, and the two women in the same scene to be her handmaidens.[[20]](#cite_note-21) He described the scene with the griffin as that of souls being tested on entry to "the Halls of the Just in the Griffin's Court", and the griffin itself as a "Chief Inquisitor".[[21]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEvans1930154-22) Evans characterised the whole scene as "the abode of light rather than of darkness", equivalent to the paradise of Elysium in later Greek mythology.[[22]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEvans1930155–156-23) [Nanno Marinatos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nanno_Marinatos "Nanno Marinatos") and Briana Jackson suggest that Evans's interpretation of the scene via Egyptian mythology, as well as his reading of the central motif as a tree, was influenced by James Frazer's *[The Golden Bough](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Golden_Bough "The Golden Bough")*, as well as by the discovery of the [Tomb of Tutankhamun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tomb_of_Tutankhamun "Tomb of Tutankhamun") in 1923.[[23]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMarinatosJackson20119–10-24)

![Grey photograph of the cast of the ring's impression: as infobox image, except the creature at the base of the tree is highly indistinct](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/55/Ring_of_Nestor_Cast_Evans_1925.png/250px-Ring_of_Nestor_Cast_Evans_1925.png)

[Martin P. Nilsson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_P._Nilsson "Martin P. Nilsson") discussed the ring in a 1927 work on Minoan and Mycenaean religion, in which he called it "a most amazing find ... [which] differs most markedly from other Mycenaean rings".[[25]](#cite_note-26)[[b]](#cite_note-27) Nilsson disagreed with Evans's association between the tree motif and the world tree, pointing out that the motif was not known to be attested prior to the eighth century CE; he considered the tree more likely to prefigure the tree in the [Garden of the Hesperides](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Garden_of_the_Hesperides "Garden of the Hesperides") in Greek mythology, which grew golden apples.[[26]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTENilsson1927550-28) In support of this, he suggested that the creature labelled by Evans as a proto-Cerberus should be considered a forerunner of [Ladon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ladon_(mythology) "Ladon (mythology)"), the dragon who guarded that tree.[[27]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTENilsson1927551-29) He considered there to be no compelling reason to suggest that the scenes on the ring were related to the afterlife or the underworld.[[28]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTENilsson1927556-30) Galanakis identifies the figure as a dragon, and considers it to be inspired by similar [Babylonian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Babylon "Babylon") motifs otherwise rare in Minoan art;[[29]](#cite_note-31) Hughes-Brock and Boardman call it a "Minoan dragon".[[30]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHughes-BrockBoardman2018449-32) Andreas Vlachopoulos identifies it as a scorpion.[[11]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEVlachopoulos2020228-12)

[Jean-Claude Poursat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean-Claude_Poursat?action=edit&redlink=1 "Jean-Claude Poursat (page does not exist)") [[fr](https://fr.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean-Claude%20Poursat "fr:Jean-Claude Poursat")], in 1976, suggested that the vertical and horizontal bands represented rivers, a hypothesis initially entertained but dismissed by Evans. In support of this, Poursat argued that the creature at the base was a "fantastical crocodile" or "crocodile-dragon". He further suggested that the lower half of the bezel, assumed to be a single episode by Evans, may have been intended to show two successive scenes.[[31]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPoursat1976472-33) Olga Krzyszkowska described Evans's interpretation of the bezel as an underworld scene as "fanciful" in 2005.[[32]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKrzyszkowska2005334-34)

## History

![Line drawing of a gold ring, in three different orientations](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a9/Ring_of_Nestor_Side_Evans_1925.png/250px-Ring_of_Nestor_Side_Evans_1925.png)

In 1907, a series of [tholos tombs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tholos_tomb "Tholos tomb") at [Kakovatos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kakovatos "Kakovatos") in [Messenia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Messenia "Messenia"), in the southwest [Peloponnese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peloponnese_(region) "Peloponnese (region)") region of Greece, were excavated by the German archaeologist [Wilhelm Dörpfeld](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wilhelm_Dörpfeld "Wilhelm Dörpfeld").[[34]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEVlachopoulos2020224–225-36) According to Evans, the ring was taken by a local peasant from one of these tombs (along with blocks of masonry) prior to the excavation, probably from the grave-pit inside the tomb's chamber.[[35]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEvans192546-37)[[c]](#cite_note-39)

In 1924, or possibly earlier, the ring was shown to the acquisitions committee of the [National Archaeological Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Archaeological_Museum,_Athens "National Archaeological Museum, Athens") in Athens, of which the German archaeologist [Georg Karo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georg_Karo "Georg Karo") was a member.[[37]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMarinatos2015194-40) Following Karo's judgement, the committee rejected the ring as a forgery, created by a modern goldsmith in the early twentieth century.[[38]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEVlachopoulos2020226-41) Evans was subsequently informed of the ring's existence by somebody he described as "a trustworthy source" (and later "a friend"): Karo inferred that Evans was referring to [Émile Gilliéron *fils*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Émile_Gilliéron_fils "Émile Gilliéron fils"), an art restorer, suspected forger, and prolific collaborator of Evans's.[[39]](#cite_note-42) Nanno Marinatos endorsed this view in 2015,[[40]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMarinatos2015194–195-43) and Vlachopoulos called it "very possible" in 2020.[[41]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEVlachopoulos2020225-44)

Evans subsequently travelled to the Peloponnese to view the ring, where he was told that the finder had died, leaving the ring to his son; the son passed it into the possession of the owner of a nearby vineyard.[[35]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEvans192546-37) Evans purchased the ring from the vineyard owner between 1924 and 1925,[[42]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEvans192546Vlachopoulos2020225-45) and named it the "Ring of Nestor" after [the mythological king](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nestor_(mythology) "Nestor (mythology)") of [the region of Messenia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Messenia_(ancient_region) "Messenia (ancient region)") in the [Homeric](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homer "Homer") poems.[[2]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMarinatosJackson20116-2) He gifted the ring to the [Ashmolean Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ashmolean_Museum "Ashmolean Museum") at the [University of Oxford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Oxford "University of Oxford") in 1939.[[2]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMarinatosJackson20116-2) It was subsequently removed from display, though placed back there in 1995.[[43]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPini19981-46) As of 2018, it remains in the Ashmolean.[[3]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHughes-BrockBoardman2018448-3)

## Debate over authenticity

The authenticity of the Ring of Nestor has been debated since its introduction to scholarship. In 2019, Angelika Hudler categorised the ring among *gemmae dubitandae* ('jewels deserving scepticism').[[d]](#cite_note-48)[[4]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHudler20194-5) In 2013, Yannis Galanakis called the ring "one of the most controversial Aegean objects in the Ashmolean's collection".[[1]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGalanakis2013159-1)

### Arguments against authenticity

Before the 1970s, most scholars considered the ring a forgery.[[45]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEliopoulos2013210-49) Nilsson, who treated the ring as genuine in 1927, revised the 1950 edition of his work to call it a "suspect object".[[46]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHudler20196-50) According to [Nanno Marinatos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nanno_Marinatos "Nanno Marinatos"), her father [Spyridon Marinatos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spyridon_Marinatos "Spyridon Marinatos") considered the Ring of Nestor a fake. She cites as evidence a reference in a 1928 letter by Marinatos to "reprimands" Evans was receiving about forgeries.[[47]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMarinatos2015190–191-51) Hagen Biesantz argued in 1954 that the ring's iconography was inconsistent with the known corpus of [Minoan art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minoan_art "Minoan art"), and accordingly that the ring was a forgery.[[48]](#cite_note-52)

![A gold ring, like the Ring of Nestor, with an oval bezel inscribed with figures. A youth climbs a hill in the centre to pick something from a tree, while two seated female figures watch.](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c1/Epiphany_cycle_%E2%80%94_THE_RING_OF_MINOS.jpg/250px-Epiphany_cycle_%E2%80%94_THE_RING_OF_MINOS.jpg)

Evans published the ring alongside the "Thisbe Treasure" from [Boeotia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boeotia "Boeotia"), considered a modern forgery, and the connection has cast doubt upon the Ring of Nestor in turn.[[32]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKrzyszkowska2005334-34) John Younger, in 1975, suggested that the ring had been forged by Gilliéron *fils* and [his father](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Émile_Gilliéron "Émile Gilliéron"), who had also been accused of forging the [Ring of Minos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ring_of_Minos?action=edit&redlink=1 "Ring of Minos (page does not exist)") apparently found at Knossos and also published by Evans.[[49]](#cite_note-53) In 1986,[[43]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPini19981-46) the Swedish archaeologist [Robin Hägg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robin_Hägg?action=edit&redlink=1 "Robin Hägg (page does not exist)") [[sv](https://sv.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robin%20Hägg "sv:Robin Hägg")] separately reported hearing from a collaborator of [Axel W. Persson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Axel_W._Persson "Axel W. Persson"), who had worked on the Aegean Bronze Age in the 1930s, that Persson had told her that Gilliéron *fils* had forged the Ring of Nestor: Hägg subsequently heard the same story from the Egyptologist [Torgny Säve-Söderbergh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Torgny_Säve-Söderbergh "Torgny Säve-Söderbergh") and from [Doro Levi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doro_Levi "Doro Levi"), director of the [Italian School of Archaeology at Athens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Italian_School_of_Archaeology_at_Athens "Italian School of Archaeology at Athens") from 1947 until 1976.[[50]](#cite_note-54) [Agnes Sakellariou](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agnes_Sakellariou?action=edit&redlink=1 "Agnes Sakellariou (page does not exist)") upheld the Gilliéron hypothesis in 1994, arguing that the insects labelled as butterflies by Evans had no direct parallels in Minoan art, but could have been based by a forger on Mycenaean examples found in tombs on the Greek mainland.[[51]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPini19983–5-55) Krzyszkowska similarly accused the Gilliérons of forging the ring in 2005.[[52]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKrzyszkowska2005p._336,_n._113-56)

Nanno Marinatos and Briana Jackson wrote in 2011 that the "complicated chain of transmission" reported to Evans raised suspicion, and made it impossible to verify the truth of the ring's discovery.[[53]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMarinatosJackson20117-57) They also argued that butterflies had no connection to the soul or reincarnation in Minoan culture, but that they were included on the ring because they held this metaphorical function in Victorian thought, and had been incorrectly linked to the concept in Mycenaean culture by [Heinrich Schliemann](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heinrich_Schliemann "Heinrich Schliemann") and more widely in Frazer's work.[[54]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMarinatosJackson201111–12-58) Marinatos and Jackson suggested that the connections between the ring's design and Egyptian iconography were based directly on *The Golden Bough*, which emphasised the religious role of oak trees and [mistletoe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mistletoe "Mistletoe"), and calculated to appeal to Evans, who had long sought to establish a relationship between Minoan religion and that of ancient Egypt.[[55]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMarinatosJackson201110-59)

### Arguments in favour of authenticity

[V. Gordon Childe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/V._Gordon_Childe "V. Gordon Childe") wrote in 1925 that "fortunately no such suspicions [of forgery] attach to the unique gold ring", and that it was "undoubtedly a remnant of the regal wealth once buried in the great tombs of Kakovatos".[[56]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChilde1925636-60)[[e]](#cite_note-62) Yiannis Sakellarakis, in 1973, considered the iconography of the ring to match other known Minoan examples, and so that the ring was likely to be genuine.[[58]](#cite_note-63) Jean-Claude Poursat accepted these arguments in his own publication of 1976.[[31]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPoursat1976472-33)

![Colourful drawing in the style of a Minoan fresco, replicating the bezel of the Ring of Nestor. The creature at the bottom of the tree is rendered as an oddly-posed dog.](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/91/Ring_of_Nestor_Drawing_Evans_1928.png/250px-Ring_of_Nestor_Drawing_Evans_1928.png)

Vlachopoulos suggests that Gilliéron could not have been involved in faking the ring, because his drawing of the bezel for Evans's publications showed a hound for the creature Vlachopoulos identified as a scorpion, demonstrating "his ignorance and his innocence".[[11]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEVlachopoulos2020228-12) [Ingo Pini](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ingo_Pini?action=edit&redlink=1 "Ingo Pini (page does not exist)") [[de](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ingo%20Pini "de:Ingo Pini")] similarly argued that the different treatment of the creature on the ring and Gilliéron's later painting of the same scene, in which Pini described the rendering as "a rather odd-looking quadruped", indicates that Gilliéron could not have made both.[[59]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPini19986-64)

Similarly, Theodore Eliopoulos suggested that the "table" on which the lion reclines as a horizontal platform supported by three incurved altars: such a platform was unknown in Minoan iconography at the time of the ring's discovery,[[60]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEliopoulos2013212–214-65) but later found in the 1970s and 1980s on frescoes from [Akrotiri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Akrotiri_(prehistoric_city) "Akrotiri (prehistoric city)"). Eliopoulos considers this evidence for a genuine Bronze Age origin.[[61]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEliopoulos2013221-66) Similarly, he argues that the appearance of lions as supporters of goddesses, known from Akrotiri frescoes as well as rings and sealings discovered after 1925, suggest the authenticity of the ring, as the lion's presence was considered anomalous when the ring was first published.[[62]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEliopoulos2013219-67) Pini argued against Sakellariou's interpretation of the butterflies as without precedent, suggesting that they echoed sealings found at the Cretan site of [Hagia Triada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hagia_Triada "Hagia Triada"), excavated in 1902–1903 but not published until 1925.[[63]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPini19985-68) He also drew a parallel between the creature at the base of the tree, which he called a "Minoan dragon", and a form on a seal found at [Mycenae](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mycenae "Mycenae") in the 1990s, while arguing that the motif would not have been known to a forger in the early twentieth century.[[59]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPini19986-64)

In 1998, [Jack Ogden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jack_Ogden_(jewellery_historian) "Jack Ogden (jewellery historian)") studied the manufacturing technique of the ring, and concluded that it matched that of genuine examples, whereby the bezel was carved first, the hoop added, and the back plate of the bezel then soldered into place. In addition, he considered that microscopic analysis of the engraving showed that it had been done according to Mycenaean techniques, which would have been unknown to an early twentieth-century forger.[[64]](#cite_note-69) Ultrasound scans of the ring presented by Walter Müller in 2002 confirmed that it was hollow, dispelling a longstanding belief that it was solid in construction, which would be unusual for a genuinely Bronze Age ring.[[65]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMüller2003480Krzyszkowska2005p._334,_n._111-70) Pini suggested that the wear on the decorations of the hoop indicates intensive use, and parallels other rings known to be genuine.[[66]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPini199810-71) Childe similarly suggested that the wear on these parts may suggest that the ring was actually worn, in contrast to Evans's belief.[[56]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChilde1925636-60)

Kate Cooper, in 2021, wrote that the ring was generally considered fake, but that the 2015 discovery of a ring (designated Ring 2) in the [Tomb of the Griffin Warrior](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tomb_of_the_Griffin_Warrior "Tomb of the Griffin Warrior"), a [shaft grave](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shaft_grave "Shaft grave") at Pylos dating to the [Late Helladic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Late_Helladic "Late Helladic") IIA period (c. 1400 – c. 1300 BCE) with similar iconography, particularly the ivy, pointed towards its authenticity.[[67]](#cite_note-72)

The images on the ring bezels depict human figures in association with epiphanic figures situated in settings characterised by the presence of [...] The many years of research that led to the present paper on the so-called Ring of Nestor (CMS VI, nο. 277), with the documentation of its authenticity, have offered me the opportunity to discuss the cases of erroneous identifications of some Creto-Mycenaean gold rings as fakes . This tendency, underpinned by the obscure – even legendary – circumstances in which these rings were found, not only the Ring of Nestor but also the Ring of Minos, has been reassessed completely in favour of their [...] The so-called Nestor Ring was found in 1924 and was accepted as authentic by Sir Arthur Evans whereas many other scholars condemned it as a forgery. In recent years, scholars have claimed its authenticity anew. This article examines the background of the find circumstances and judges them suspicious. ## Abstract

![Image 10: sparkles](https://a.academia-assets.com/images/icons/sparkle.svg)
AI

This paper presents an analysis of the iconography surrounding the 'Ring of Nestor' in the context of Aegean forgeries and authenticity debates. By revisiting key iconographic features and comparisons, the paper aims to contribute to the ongoing discourse regarding the ring's significance in Minoan and Mycenaean art. Observations draw upon historical scholarship and recent discoveries to question and affirm previous conclusions related to the ring's motifs and their implications.

[Towards a Consideration of Unprovenanced Ancient and Medieval Finger Rings](https://www.academia.edu/37745254/Towards_a_Consideration_of_Unprovenanced_Ancient_and_Medieval_Finger_Rings)

[TN Pollio](https://independent.academia.edu/TNPollio)

This article will hopefully incentivize researchers to consider examining the untoward thousands of unprovenanced base metal and silver alloy finger rings being uncovered at sites from the U.K to Eurasia. Documented artifacts from controlled and stratified environments are of course essential towards understanding ring typology and routes of transmission across temporal and spatial environments. However, these standard methodologies should not preclude consideration of random and under-documented finds from non-professional sources. The rationale is simply that, within the last several decades, a significant proportion of new finds have in fact been made through amateur channels; and the rings they've uncovered may potentially contribute to our understanding of these underreported artifacts. Within the last few decades, the proliferation of metal detecting and use of the internet have ensured the issue is no longer of availability, but identity. The era of scarcity is obviously over, in view of the burgeoning array of base metal rings encountered on the international market. Any a priori disqualification of such a vast resource of emerging data is to ignore an untapped resource towards our understanding of ancient societies and the material culture associated therewith The need for reliable and broadly accessible reference material becomes increasingly apparent as more and more finger rings are uncovered and presented through on-line and other sources. Types which were once familiar only to academics have suddenly flooded the public conscience; but with little increase in resources towards the understanding of these artifacts. Small finds such as bronze finger rings are routinely uncovered at archaeological sites in Europe, North Africa, the Middle East and Eurasia. They are typically noted in excavation reports, then cataloged and archived in places such as universities and museums. Unfortunately, both the reports and rings themselves are rarely accessible in mediums available to the general public. In most cases, only other professionals – such as academics and historians – are even aware of their existence. In terms of accessibility, most of this research has been compiled in unfamiliar languages and arcane formats which, to the general public, might as well be written in cuneiform and buried on the dark side of the moon. Many in English speaking countries have some proficiency in languages such as French, German and Spanish. But how many would understand technical reports written in Russian, Polish, Slovak, Bulgarian, Serbian, Romanian, Hungarian, Turkish or Greek – the languages in which much of this research has been published? Unfamiliar languages and limited/restricted formats are significant impediments toward the dissemination of this otherwise invaluable material.

[One Ring to Know Them All: An Experimental Approach to Reconstructing the 'Ring of Hermes'](https://www.academia.edu/122737531/One_Ring_to_Know_Them_All_An_Experimental_Approach_to_Reconstructing_the_Ring_of_Hermes)

[Marios Koutsoukos](https://liverpool.academia.edu/MariosKoutsoukos)

Work In Progress, 2023

In Late Antiquity, no Roman would think twice about questioning the efficacy of ceremonial magic. They might doubt its legitimacy or, perhaps, the methods of the magician, but no one would ever dismiss magic itself as an operative force in the cosmos as well as a direct means of interacting with divine powers. Its potential efficacy was an accepted reality of life for layman and philosopher alike. It is in this cultural milieu that magical formularies such as those preserved in the Greek Magical Papyri circulated amongst ritual experts and Platonic philosophers with an affinity towards theurgy. What was the magical praxis like from the perspective of the operator? How did it enable a direct interaction with divine powers from a lived ancient religions point of view? When addressing these questions, modern scholarship very often confines itself in the traditional approach of textual examination, relying on individual accounts, such as that of the first-century Greek physician Thessalos of Tralles. or second-hand narratives, like those in Porphyry’s Life of Plotinus. The present paper proposes a hybrid method of studying Late Antique magical formularies which combines the methodology of textual approach with that of experimental archaeology. Termed experimental ritualism, this approach is presented through an experiment in reconstructing the magic ‘Ring of Hermes’ (PGM 213-303). This paper uses self-reflection to trace the process from the construction of the physical object itself to its ritual consecration and the attempts at putting the ring to its intended use. In effect, it is not merely the record of an experimental reconstruction but also an attempt at empirically adopting as emic a perspective as possible towards Late Antique magic praxis. Keywords: Graeco-Egyptian Magic; Greek Magical Papyri; Late Antiquity; Experimental Archaeology; Theurgy; Magic Ring.

The task of attributing seals to different hands or workshops is still a desideratum in Aegean studies, for the identification of Aegean seal-engravers and goldsmiths and their stylistic output could dramatically change our knowledge of the use, circulation and social impact of certain seals or seal groups and refine our methods of dating this (often only roughly datable) medium. A set of new data and methods now available, such as precise measurements of sizes and weights, x-ray analysis and material analysis finally enable us to shed new light on several questions concerning individual styles and thus to identify " masters " without the usual reliance on iconography. [Yoav Farhi](https://eretzmuseum.academia.edu/YoavFarhi)

Jerusalem Journal of Archaeology

This paper presents a rare bronze finger ring that was found more than half a century ago and bears a symbol known mainly from the coins of Mattathias Antigonus. A teenager recovered it from one of the burial caves in the cliff of Naḥal David at ‘En Gedi. Although the cave was later excavated by Nahman Avigad, the ring was forgotten and was not incorporated in the excavation report. This paper discusses the ring, the symbol it bears, and its relation to the coins of Antigonus. I suggest a date and identification for the burials in the cave that associates them with the conflict between Herod and Antigonus.

What explains the authenticity debate surrounding the ring of Nestor?add

The research highlights that the ring's authenticity was primarily defended by Sakellarakis in 1971 due to iconographic elements like butterflies and griffin-headed women, despite earlier skepticism from many scholars.

How do incurved altars relate to the ring of Nestor's iconography?add

The study proposes that the platform depicted in the ring is supported by incurved altars, mirroring construction styles revealed by the Xeste 3 fresco, unknown to scholars until the 1970s.

When was the ring of Nestor first published and what was its initial reception?add

Published in 1925, the ring was initially viewed with skepticism regarding its authenticity, with many scholars attributing it to a forger's work due to perceived inconsistencies.

How did the research address previous skepticism about the ring of Nestor?add

The paper counters past arguments by demonstrating specific iconographic parallels, such as those identified in the Archanes excavation, revealing a strong cultural connection absent in forgery narratives.

What implications does the ring's iconography have for understanding ancient Aegean culture?add

The findings suggest a rich interplay between religious practices and artistic representations, as seen through elements like the lion, which may represent royal or divine power within ceremonial contexts.
